Source: http://www.press.co.nz

Posted June 20, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: This is a good attempt at honest journalism. As you will see, I have some problems with this article, but there is no reefer madness here.)
June 19, 2000
From The Christchurch Press
editorial@press.co.nz
http://www.press.co.nz/
By Greg Scanlon

POT: HOW FAR TO GO?

Supporters of cannabis decriminalisation claim that it would free the police to spend more time on more pertinent issues, but the police see big problems with harder drugs if too many changes are made. GLEN SCANLON reports.

'If there is indeed a war on drugs, it is not being won. Drugs are demonstrably cheaper and more easily available than ever before.

" If a sufficiently large, and apparently growing, part of the population chooses to ignore the law for whatever reason, then that law becomes unenforceable. "

If you think these are the words of a Left-wing liberal pot-smoking politician, you could not be more wrong.

Britain's Cleveland police force made the comments in a report it compiled on drug use last year.

The report finds there is no apparent logic in making tobacco and alcohol available when cannabis is seen as less harmful by many scientists. It says the police may find themselves powerless to prevent illegal activity under present laws.
See
Great London Times Column and News From New Zealand Compare Marijuana and Alcohol
and
David Hadorn Writes:
Beyond A Reasonable Doubt Cannabis Is Substantially Less Harmful Than Alcohol Or Tobacco.

Our own police recommended to the Government last year that priority be given to considering the use of infringement notices for offences such as cannabis possession to save money and time.

The police spent more than 300,000 hours and $22 million on enforcing cannabis laws last year. That was 120,000 hours more and nearly double what they spent in 1992-1993.

Nearly 8000 people were prosecuted for cannabis possession. Another 3000 were given warnings or diversion, or handled by the youth justice system.
(MarijuanaNews note: New Zealand’s population is less than 4 million, so it may have the highest per capita marijuana arrest rate in the world. It is sad that while everyone worries about the effects of marijuana, so little thought is given to the effects of being arrested.)
See
Australian Study Shows Marijuana Laws Not A Deterrent To Use,
But They Often Wreck Lives:
" The health risks of cannabis use were often debated in the media
but little was said about the social harms associated with a conviction. " -- 2 Articles

Under the present law a person can be arrested for possessing the tiniest amount of cannabis. Users and the odd dealer clog the court system, many returning over and over again.

Punishments range from small fines to three months in prison for possession. Dealing in the drug attracts a much higher punishment.

Supporters of decriminalisation claim, rather simplistically, that the police are wasting a lot of time, which could be spent on more pertinent problems such as burglary and serious crime.
(MarijuanaNews note: Simplistic? Perhaps, but it is not just the police who are wasting time. The resources of the entire criminal justice system are finite.)
See
New Zealand Police Minister On the Marijuana Laws:
" My own personal feeling is that it is costing a huge amount of police time at the moment. "
NZ Psychologist Remembers Being Arrested Ten Years Ago For Saying That He Smoked.
– 2 Articles

They often point the finger, accusing the police of using cannabis to hold or harass individuals who use it for medicinal or recreational purposes.

The police reject the claims, saying that only those suspected of committing crimes can be arrested, and that harassing offenders is illegal.
(MarijuanaNews note: And the police would never break the law? Are things that different in New Zealand?)
See
New Zealand Narcs Attack Police Minister For Encouraging Them To Smoke Undercover
While He Is Saying That Marijuana Is Harmful. Who Is Fooling Whom, Other Than The Editor?

Assistant police commissioner Paul Fitzharris says the police typically " fall over " cannabis offences in the course of other work.
See
New Zealand Pays Former Narcs Compensation For Being " Marijuana Addicts "
– No, This Is Not An April Fools Joke!

He repeats the police line on cannabis: " The policy at the moment is that the use and possession of cannabis is prohibited by the law, and it is our job to enforce the law. "

Individual constables, however, use their discretion when dealing with cannabis users, says Mr Fitzharris.

University of Canterbury criminologist Dr Greg Newbold says some officers have told him that they already ignore more than 50 per cent of use.

Mr Fitzharris says the police are trying to get away from individual opinions, and form a policy on possible changes to the cannabis law.

He believes that no one is advocating complete legalisation, which could result in cannabis being available over the counter, and large-scale production allowed.
(MarijuanaNews note: " No one is advocating complete legalization "? He should know better. Surely he does.)
See
A Major Contribution -- Regulate And Tax Cannabis --
Full Text of New Zealand Drug Policy Forum Final Report

The police are considering several options, he says, including " depenalisation " for small possession offences.

This could include a system of warnings and diversion, which would not require a law change.

Infringement notices are another option, but they would need a law change, which would bring its own problems.

Infringement notices would require enforcement, which would cost money and throw people back into the court system. This is not the goal desired, as South Australia recently discovered.

A review of its 13-year-old system of issuing infringement notices found that a lot of young and poor people ended up with convictions because they were unable to pay fines.

Moreover, it is almost impossible to calculate what the effect on price and supply will be of the above options, says Mr Fitzharris. The police approach now is to target dealers, but changes may mean more time and money are available to attack them and big growers.
(MarijuanaNews note: If it is true that if the police stopped arresting users, they would have more time to go after growers and dealers, then why isn’t it true that they would also have more time to spend " on more pertinent problems such as burglary and serious crime, " which we were just told above is " simplistic "?)

Police Association president Greg O'Connor, who has no problem with recreational use by adults, sees greater problems if too many changes are made.

He believes too much change will cause the price of cannabis to drop, while also increasing the market, because a lot more people will grow their own.

" Gangs in New Zealand are a little like the mafia in the United States, which grew up on alcohol prohibition.

 " When it was legalised, they didn't go away. They just moved on to other forms of illicit income, " he says.
See
New Zealand Landowner Offers A Different Reason To Oppose Marijuana Prohibition

Mr O'Connor believes the gangs will shift production to more profitable drugs such as methamphetamines, which are the drug of choice overseas.

Plenty of information is available on the Internet detailing how $1000 of chemicals can be turned into $10,000 of drugs.

Dr Newbold, who wants some liberalisation, agrees with Mr O'Connor.

He believes, depending how far the changes go, that the price of cannabis will drop, and the supply will increase because the police will be spending less time spraying and destroying plants.

If the price does not hold, the gangs will probably move to other drugs such as Ecstasy, methamphetamines, and LSD, says Dr Newbold.
(MarijuanaNews note: There are actually two arguments here, both of which are used by prohibitionists around the world.

The first argument is that if marijuana is legalized, then organized crime will just get into other areas. Here this argument seems to be taken even further, suggesting that the marijuana markets should be left to organized crime to prevent them from doing something worse.

There are three big problems with this line.

First, keeping marijuana illegal does not prevent criminals from getting involved in other areas. In fact, most of the synthetic drugs offer much larger profits than does cannabis, so they already have a strong incentive to get into these areas, and they are.
See
Prohibitionist UK -- Not Holland -- Leads Europe In Illegal Drug Production.
But This Does Not Fit the Prohibitionist Party Line

In fact, marijuana prohibition gives them access to a very large group of buyers to whom they try to sell these more profitable drugs. This is one reason why the Dutch believe in the " separation of the markets. "

See
An Official Statement On The Netherlands’ Drug
Policy; Published In The Most Improbable Place

Second, marijuana prohibition creates a huge contraband market with a total lack of quality controls, age restrictions, and a potential for police corruption. Legal markets have far fewer such problems.

Third, it is unjust to force marijuana users to have to depend on the contraband markets, while alcohol and tobacco users have access to legal products with controlled quality.

The second line is that legalization will cause prices to fall and thereby increase usage, which they think would be a bad thing. I will deal with that below.)

Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis Party spokesman and lawyer Michael Appleby disagrees. He believes cannabis prices will remain high because a lot of people will not grow their own.

The price can vary from $250 an ounce to $600 an ounce depending on the time of year.
(MarijuanaNews note: The New Zealand dollar is around 48 US cents.)

Experiences overseas are probably the best source of information, but it is often conflicting and contradictory.

Countries such as Italy, Spain, and the Netherlands have depenalised the use of cannabis, with the Dutch example the most researched.

The Dutch have allowed the personal use of cannabis since 1976, but still aggressively target large-scale growers and dealers, which keeps the price high.
(MarijuanaNews note: Because of its prohibitionist neighbors, the Dutch try to suppress large-scale operations, but marijuana growing is a huge cottage industry in Holland, as it is in Canada – and even in DEAland. Most of the cannabis consumed by the Dutch smokers is not bought in the coffee shops, but grown by the user.

This fact also argues against the claim that the coffee shops are responsible for any increase in the rate of marijuana use there. It was increasing everywhere, and the Dutch like to grow their own.

Also, the cost of marijuana sold by the gram in a coffee shop is the price of the smallest unit of sale and includes the conveninece and the use of the shop for smoking. In any case, the price of a gram of good – but not the best -- marijuana in a Dutch coffee shop is around US$5.00, and a gram in Vancouver is around US$7.00.

Wholesale Dutch prices are around half of retail, or around US$1,250 per pound. This is close to the wholesale price in Vancouver, where the market is currently weak for all except the best marijuana.

When a product is sold by the gram, prices will tend to remain relatively high, regardless of legal status. Handling and transaction costs will keep prices up.

Because marijuana is both easy and pleasant to grow, those who smoke a lot will try to grow their own, if they can. But not everyone can. In any case, arresting people for growing their own marijuana is incredibly bad social police. It forces them into the black market.

People go to coffee shops for both convenience and social setting. After all, people can buy beer much more cheaply in stores than at bars, but people still go to bars, paying many times more for a drink than it would cost at home. And marijuana is a supremely social drug.)

Small amounts of cannabis can be bought from up to 1500 coffee shops across the Netherlands.

The Dutch experience is often trumpeted by pro-cannabis groups as a success, but some studies have discovered problems in Nirvana.
See
Chairman of The Youth Trust of New Zealand Parrots DEAland Lies About Dutch. Whom Can Youth Trust?

One found that from 1984 to 1996 the prevalence of cannabis use climbed sharply. In 1984, 15 per cent of people aged 18 to 20 had used the drug. This rose to 44 per cent by 1996.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is one of the prohibitionists’ favorite lines, but there are two problems here. The first is that the 1984 number is probably wrong, but never mind. The bigger problem is the assumption of causality, that Dutch marijuana use went up because of the existence of the coffee shops. Marijuana use has increased in other European countries as well, and as it happens, Dutch marijuana use is still below that in most countries with marijuana prohibition.
See
 " The failure of Dutch drug policy " An Examination of Prohibitionist Propaganda and the Official Dutch Government Response -- Special To MarijuanaNews

Also, 1979 was supposedly the peak year for marijuana use in DEAland and the prohibitionists like to say that marijuana use was going down in DEAland during the 1980s while it was going up in Holland.

This neatly overlooks the crack cocaine epidemic in DEAland, which the Dutch did not have. Thus, declining marijuana use in the 1980s did not prove that DEAland policies were more successful than the Dutch. Even in 1991, supposedly the low point for DEAland marijuana use, the Dutch rate was below that of DEAland. New Zealand has even higher rates of use.)
See
Reefer Madness in New Zealand Op-ed Says " We Are Killing Our Kids With Cannabis'. " And A Little Prohibitionist Humor.

The biggest users were young people from wide backgrounds, including tourists, a point of contention in relations with France, Germany, and Belgium, which have complained that they are being flooded with drugs from the Netherlands.

No link between cannabis and the use of harder drugs was found.
See
British Columbia Court Rules Two to One That Marijuana Possession Laws Must Be Decided By Parliament. Dissent Makes Hearing By Supreme Court Likely. Facts Make Marijuana Prohibition Look Bad, Again.

In 1995 the Dutch dropped the amount that people were allowed to possess from 30g to 5g because of domestic and international pressure.
(MarijuanaNews note: No, they dropped the amount that shops are allowed to sell to 5 grams per customer. The Dutch police never arrest people with 30 grams.)

Figures from the British Medical Journal, however, say that the monthly prevalence of cannabis use among Dutch students is 5.4 per cent, compared with 29 per cent in the United States.

Mr Fitzharris says the effect any changes will have on the level of use and risk to the community, particularly young people, is one of the biggest concerns.

Mr O'Connor says he does not want teenagers gaining easier access, or cannabis becoming so acceptable that it is smoked outside offices.
See
New Zealand Minister Denounces Hypocrisy Of Politicians
Who Abuse Alcohol But Condemn Young People For Marijuana

(MarijuanaNews note: It seems unlikely that access to marijuana could get much easier for teens, especially in New Zealand. If a child there is not using marijuana now, it is not because he cannot find it.)

Mr Appleby does not believe depenalisation will increase use dramatically.
See
California Bureaucracy Suppresses Report Showing Marijuana Use Among California Students Leveled Off After Passage Of Prop 215. Meanwhile, In New Zealand, Prohbitionists Use The Same Party Line.

(MarijuanaNews note: Perhaps, but anti-prohibitionists should not fall into the trap accepting that any increase in marijuana use would be a bad thing.

First, as noted, it would be unlikely that teen use would increase very much, inasmuch as they can already get all they want, and it will still be illegal to sell to youths.

Second, an increase in use by adults – and even teens – would be a good thing if that meant less alcohol use by them.

Third, a substantial increase by older citizens might be a very good thing, if that meant less dependence on expensive and dangerous pharmaceuticals.

Finally, marijuana use could soar enormously and it still would not be a burden on the public health that was even close to the burden caused by alcohol and tobacco.)
See
The Reality Of the Marijuana Situation In Canada: Unequal Injustice.
Alcohol Costs Canadian Health Almost 100 Times As Much As Marijuana.
Tobacco: Almost 200 As Much – Article and Editorial

Mr Fitzharris expects the police will finish their research and form a view in a couple of months.
(MarijuanaNews note: One hopes that they will be a little better informed when they do.)

Whatever happens, the one guarantee is that a high level of cannabis use will continue.As Mr O'Connor says, cannabis used recreationally is a good mood-enhancing drug. " We've got to start by acknowledging that people enjoy it. "
